# Security Testing and Code Review (TEST)

## SCS-TEST-01 Include security scenarios in functional, integration and UAT testing

Level: MUST

Applies to: All (Flutter and Backend)

Policy: Functional and integration testing before every production release MUST include security scenarios. Authentication, authorization and data protection MUST be validated during UAT.

Implementation (all stacks):

- Minimum scenarios: access without login, access as the wrong role, access to another user's record (IDOR), invalid and oversized input, expired and tampered tokens, logout and session expiry.

Implementation (.NET / SQL Server):

- Integration tests with WebApplicationFactory covering 401/403/404 responses for each role, plus validation failures.

Verification: Test plan and UAT test cases include the security scenarios; results are attached to the release record.

## SCS-TEST-02 Run standard code evaluation tools on your own code before submitting

Level: SHOULD

Applies to: All (Flutter and Backend)

Policy: Developers SHOULD run the standard code evaluation tools below on their own code before opening a merge request or submitting it for security review, fix what they can, and attach the results. This self-check catches common weaknesses early. It is advice to developers; responsibility for evaluating security stays with the Security Reviewer (SCS-TEST-03).

Implementation (all stacks):

- Secrets: gitleaks (gitleaks git -v, or gitleaks dir . for an uncommitted folder) on the repository before pushing; ideally as a pre-commit hook (SCS-SEC-03).
- Static analysis: SonarQube Community Build or SonarQube for IDE (SonarLint) with the security rules on, for both C# and Dart.
- Dependencies: osv-scanner scan source -r . on the repository (reads pubspec.lock and packages.lock.json).
- Record the tool names, versions and a summary of the results (or attach the reports) in the merge request.

Implementation (.NET / SQL Server):

- dotnet build with the .NET analyzers on (<AnalysisMode>Recommended</AnalysisMode>), including the CA5xxx security rules and EF1002; never suppress them without a written reason.
- dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive.
- For web apps and APIs: an OWASP ZAP baseline scan of your build in the test environment.

Verification: Merge requests include the self-check results. The Security Reviewer notes in the Security Review Report whether they were received.

Current gap: IT-56 ASR-34 and IT-57 §11 #1, #2 and #4 record SAST, dependency scanning and secret-scanning hooks as planned, not yet in place. Until they are added to the CI pipeline, developers run them locally.

## SCS-TEST-03 Security Reviewer evaluates security and reports every weakness found

Level: MUST

Applies to: All (Flutter and Backend)

Policy: The Security Reviewer is responsible for evaluating the security of every application this section develops before its first release, and of every change before it goes to production. The review MUST be done on the source code in the application's private Git repository, to which the Security Reviewer is invited, and MUST follow this technique: (1) a local LLM evaluates the codebase against this standard; (2) optionally, a second-opinion review is done with Claude; (3) the Security Reviewer manually reviews the LLM report and the code. Only findings confirmed in the manual review are reported. The Security Reviewer MUST then add a Security Review Report (Appendix B) to the repository that lists every weakness found, with its severity, location, broken policy, and raise one repository issue per finding. Applications developed by external vendors are not reviewed under this policy; they are assessed under SCS-SUP-04.

Implementation (all stacks):

- Scope: the changes in the release (from the merge requests and change record), plus any area labeled "security-review"; the whole application for a first release, a major change or a High-risk application.
- Access: the application's developers invite the Security Reviewer to its private Git repository (read access, personal account with MFA). The review covers a stated branch and commit. Source code is not sent by email or copied to shared drives for review.
- Step 1, local LLM evaluation: a locally hosted LLM evaluates the codebase against this standard (give it the Markdown edition for the stack and the Appendix A checklist) and produces a draft list of weaknesses. The code stays on Juhayna-controlled machines.
- Step 2, second opinion (optional): Claude may be used for a second-opinion review.
- Step 3, manual review: read the LLM output and the code, confirm or reject each finding in the code, and check the areas LLMs often miss: authorization and object ownership, business logic, authentication flows, secrets, error handling, logging, file upload and configuration. Review the threat model and the Appendix A checklist. LLM output is a draft; the Security Reviewer is accountable for the report.
- Supporting tools: also run gitleaks and a dependency scan (osv-scanner, dotnet list package --vulnerable), because an LLM cannot reliably find every secret or known-vulnerable package version. Run an OWASP ZAP scan on the test environment for web apps and APIs where practical.
- Rate each finding (Critical / High / Medium / Low / Informational, with a CVSS score), link it to the SCS policy and CWE it breaks, and give a fix. Do not put real secrets or personal data in the report.
- Add the report to the repository (docs/security-reviews/), raise one issue per finding labeled "security" with its severity and the due date from SCS-OPS-01, and notify the developers and the Section Head. Re-test fixed findings and update the report and the issues.

Implementation (.NET / SQL Server):

- Backend evaluation also covers configuration for the target environment (appsettings, IIS/Kestrel, CORS, headers), SQL Server permissions and stored procedures, and SAP service user authorizations.

Verification: A Security Review Report exists in the repository for each release, covering the commit that is deployed, with each finding raised as a repository issue.

## SCS-TEST-04 Get final security approval from the Security Reviewer before production

Level: MUST

Applies to: All (Flutter and Backend)

Policy: An application or change MUST NOT be deployed to production without the Security Reviewer's written approval, recorded in the Security Review Report in the application's repository and linked from the release change record. Approval applies only to the exact version and commit evaluated. It MUST NOT be given while Critical or High findings are open, unless an approved exception covers them. Medium and Low findings may remain open only with due dates under SCS-OPS-01.

Implementation (all stacks):

- Release order: developer self-check (SCS-TEST-02), then merge, then Security Reviewer evaluation and report (SCS-TEST-03), then fixes and re-test, then security approval, then the Section Head's release approval and deployment (SCS-DEP-02).
- Decisions are Approved, Approved with conditions (listed with due dates), or Rejected.
- Any code or configuration change after approval needs a new evaluation of that change and a new approval before it is deployed.
- Emergency fixes: the Security Reviewer reviews and approves the fix before deployment where possible; otherwise within 2 working days after it, as part of the emergency change review (SCS-DEP-02).
- The deployment pipeline or the release checklist checks that the commit being deployed matches the approved commit in the report.

Verification: For each production deployment, the change record links a Security Review Report whose approved commit matches the deployed commit.
